indescribable

/in-duh-SKRIY-buh-bul/ — stress on SKRIY · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Indescribable describes something so extreme that ordinary words cannot fully capture it.

The smell of the harbor's fish market at low tide was indescribable.

Example

When the avalanche swept past the climbers, survivors could only describe the roar as indescribable — no sound they had ever heard compared to it.

Indescribable is precise because it suggests the thing is so extreme and intense that language itself breaks down. Words like 'loud' or 'overwhelming' just mean strong or hard to handle; indescribable captures the special sense that no words exist to capture this.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

unspeakable: Unspeakable means too terrible to talk about — it clings to horrors, crimes, and grief, things people cannot bear to name. Indescribable carries no such judgment: a view, a joy, or a roar can be indescribable simply because ordinary words are not big enough for it.

breathtaking: Breathtaking means so beautiful or astonishing that it stuns you for a moment — the word points at your gasp. Indescribable points at your silence afterward: the experience is so extreme that words fail when you try to tell anyone what it was like.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

ordinary: usual, common, and easy to describe

mundane: dull and everyday, with nothing special

Where it sits · how far beyond normal experience it goes

remarkable → extraordinary → overwhelming → indescribable

remarkable vs. indescribable: Remarkable is the mildest step toward indescribable: remarkable means worth noticing, while indescribable means so extreme that words fail completely.

extraordinary vs. indescribable: Extraordinary is stronger than remarkable but still weaker than indescribable: extraordinary goes far beyond normal, yet it can still be put into words — the indescribable cannot.

overwhelming vs. indescribable: Overwhelming comes closest to indescribable: an overwhelming experience floods your senses, while an indescribable one floods them so completely that language gives out.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-: not (Latin)

Prefix — de-: down, thoroughly (Latin)

Root — scrib (from scribere): to write (Latin)

Suffix — -able: can be done (Latin)

Put it together: In- ('not') + de- ('down') + scrib ('write') + -able ('can be done') builds 'not able to be written down' — indescribable describes something so extreme that ordinary words cannot fully capture it.

Use the root in a new word: scribble: The toddler loved to scribble on every page — scribble comes from Latin scribere, 'to write,' the same root hiding in indescribable, 'not able to be written down in words.'

Word Choice

formal / literary

Indescribable is for things so extreme that ordinary words break down. Reach for it when the experience or sensation is genuinely beyond language — a view that stuns, a joy that has no name. For something merely impressive or difficult to express, 'extraordinary' or 'hard to describe' is usually simpler and more honest.
